newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chubais promises cash as Russia braces for protests.
newsitem.headline: Chubais promises cash as Russia braces for protests.

text.p: Russia's new economy supremo Anatoly Chubais pledged on Friday to pay off massive arrears in wages and pensions as the government went on the offensive to defuse nationwide strikes and protests planned for next week.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who kept his job this week when President Boris Yeltsin brought in a new, young cabinet team, was due to confront a hostile parliament at 4 p.m. (1300 GMT) to explain the reorganisation.

As Yeltsin sat down in Helsinki with U.S. President Bill Clinton for summit talks focusing on NATO expansion, First Deputy Prime Minister Chubais was in Kemerovo, Siberia, to address the national coalminers' union. The miners were among Yeltsin's most loyal backers in the early 1990s but are disenchanted with reform.

Bearing a personal message of goodwill from Yeltsin and some $30 million in back wages for the local Kuzbass region, Chubais, who is also finance minister, pledged to pay all wage arrears by the end of the year and clear the pensions backlog before June 30.

Playing down the importance of planned strikes on March 27, the 41-year-old economist who earned the hatred of communists for his post-Soviet privatisation drive, told the miners the new government had solutions -- but needed more time.
"We (the government) will take responsibility on ourselves," he said. "And if the Russian people put their trust in us for a little while, then today's very severe problems will be solved.
"Now, as never before, we have a chance to turn the situation around in favour of the Russian people," he was quoted by Itar-Tass news agency as telling protestors from mining areas.
"There is little left to do -- to push out the rest of the pensions and wages, get rid of delays."
Russian workers are owed about 50 trillion roubles ($8.8 billion) in back wages, of which 10 trillion is owed by the state, which is struggling with low tax collection.
Union leader Vitaly Budko said the miners were the worst hit of the public sector workers, owed some 2.7 trillion roubles.

In Moscow, Labour Minister Gennady Melikyan met employers' leader Vladimir Kolmagorov and labour leader Mikhail Shmakov to discuss smoothing the transfer of money out to the provinces to pay off arrears and ease tensions before March 27, Tass said.
"We realise there is real hardship in the country but we understand also the enormous danger of rocking the boat any further, since events could get out of control," Melikyan said.
Shmakov's Federation of Independent Trade Union has said seven million members will join in protests next Thursday.
Some opposition leaders say the planned events of March 27 could serve as a catalyst for Albanian-style anarchy, although recent labour protests in Russia have been tame affairs.
Union leaders have already softened their demands for a change of government since the reshuffle.
Ahead of Friday's parliamentary appearance, Chernomyrdin tried on Thursday to defuse tensions between the government and the Duma (lower house), which is dominated by the communists and their allies.
"The government will cooperate with the State Duma in a constructive way," he told leaders of the main parties.
The Duma invited Chernomyrdin to appear before it on Friday to explain the government changes.
Despite its loud criticism, it has no power to challenge the reshuffle because the prime minister himself remained in place.
The assembly may also debate a non-binding anti-NATO resolution, declaring that Russia would never become part of the bloc. It is one of the few issues that unites the Kremlin and the Duma.
